extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics; readers studying Kant's Critique of Judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's criteria for aesthetic judgement (what makes something beautiful, pleasant, or good), including disinterestedness, universality, and the free play of cognitive faculties. Useful for analyzing or teaching Kantian aesthetics and distinguishing aesthetic from cognitive/practical judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste is aesthetical (subjective determining ground)
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to decide whether anything is beautiful or not, we refer the representation ... by the Imagination (perhaps in conjunction with the Understanding) to the subject, and its feeling of pleasure or pain. The judgement of taste is therefore not a judgement of cognition, and is consequently not logical but aesthetical, ... whose determining ground can be no other than subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgement of taste refers representations to the subject's feeling (pleasure/pain), not to the object for cognition. It does not increase cognitive knowledge of the object; it compares the representation with the subject's whole faculty of representations. Thus when evaluating beauty, do not treat the judgement as cognitive or concept-based; treat it as an aesthetic, subjective assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of the satisfaction that determines taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction which determines the judgement of taste is disinterested. When the question is if a thing is beautiful, we do not want to know whether anything depends on the existence of the thing either for myself or for any one else, but how we judge it by mere observation (intuition or reflection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pure judgement of taste must be made with indifference to the object's existence or practical value. Any mingling of personal interest (desire for the object's existence, social vanity, usefulness) renders the judgement partial and not a pure aesthetic judgement. Examples in text: preferring cook-shops, rejecting palaces for moral reasons—such interests disqualify a pure judgement of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantness is bound up with interest (not pure taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: That which pleases the senses in sensation is PLEASANT. The satisfaction in the Pleasant is bound up with interest: it excites a desire for objects of that kind; consequently the satisfaction presupposes the relation of its existence to my state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate 'pleasant' with 'beautiful'. Pleasantness arises from sensory gratification and generates inclination/desire; judgements that express mere gratification are empirical and private. When evaluating, identify whether approval is tied to sensory desire (pleasant) rather than disinterested aesthetic pleasure (beautiful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good is conceptually bound and tied to interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever by means of Reason pleases through the mere concept is GOOD. The good involves the concept of a purpose, and consequently the relation of Reason to possible volition, and thus a satisfaction in the presence of an object (some kind of interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodness is evaluated through concepts and practical reason (usefulness/ moral worth). To call something 'good' presupposes a concept of what the object ought to be and relates to will/volition. Distinguish evaluative claims grounded in concepts and purposes (good) from aesthetic, non-conceptual claims (beautiful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold distinction: Pleasant vs Beautiful vs Good
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pleasant, the Beautiful, and the Good designate three different relations of representations to the feeling of pleasure and pain: that which GRATIFIES is called pleasant; that which merely PLEASES is beautiful; that which is ESTEEMED or approved (objective worth) is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a work or object, classify the kind of satisfaction it provides: sensory gratification (pleasant), disinterested aesthetic pleasure (beautiful), or concept-based/practical/moral worth (good). The text gives examples (food = pleasant, flowers = beautiful, moral actions = good) and warns against conflating categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty of judging of an object or a method of representing it by an entirely disinterested satisfaction or dissatisfaction. The object of such satisfaction is called beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition as the operational test for 'taste': does the judgement rest on entirely disinterested satisfaction? If yes, the faculty at work is taste and the object may be called beautiful. Emphasize contemplative attitude and absence of concept-driven or desire-driven motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty = object represented as the object of universal satisfaction apart from concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful is that which apart from concepts is represented as the object of a universal satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgement of beauty claims a kind of universal assent even though it is not grounded in concepts. In practice, calling something 'beautiful' implies expecting others to share the same disinterested pleasure. When evaluating claims of beauty, check for this implicit claim to universal communicability despite lack of conceptual justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic universality is subjective (subjective universal validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality of the satisfaction is represented in a judgement of Taste only as subjective. The judgement imputes agreement to everyone but this universality does not rest on concepts of objects and so is not logical but aesthetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'subjective universality' (aesthetic claim that others ought to share the pleasure) from 'objective (logical) universality' which rests on concepts. Recognize that aesthetic claims demand a 'universal voice' without offering conceptual reasons—this is a feature, not a logical flaw, of judgements of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free play of cognitive faculties grounds the judgement and precedes pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective universal communicability of the representation must be fundamental, and must have the pleasure in the object as its consequent. This subjective condition is the state of free play of Imagination and Understanding in a representation, and the pleasure is grounded in the harmony of these cognitive faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing aesthetic responses, look for evidence that the perceived beauty arises from a felt harmony or 'free play' between imagination and understanding (not from application of a determinate concept). The judgement (awareness of this harmonious play) precedes and causes the pleasure, rather than pleasure merely being reported and then generalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness without purpose (formal purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be purposiveness without purpose: purposiveness according to form can be noticed in objects though we do not place the causes of this form in a will; we can observe a purposiveness according to form without basing it on a purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgement often attributes a kind of purposiveness (forma finalis) to an object's form though no actual purpose or design is presupposed. In evaluating beauty, consider whether the form appears 'purposive' in a way intelligible to reason even if no concrete purpose is intended—this perceived purposiveness is central to Kant's account of aesthetic response.
